newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: CRICKET-Rixon blames rain rules for NZ 1-day loss.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-Rixon blames rain rules for NZ 1-day loss.

text.p: NAPIER, Feb 26 - New Zealand's rain-affected second one-day cricket loss to England last Sunday shouldn't have gone ahead, according to Kiwi coach Steve Rixon.
It was the latest example of a limited-overs international which required a version of rain rules to produce a result.
Having made 253 for eight in their 50 overs, New Zealand fancied their chances of levelling the five-game series.
After England had reached 47 without loss off six overs, rain -- which had been forecast in the days leading up to the match -- arrived.
Play stopped for one-and-three-quarter hours, which meant match officials had to get out their calculators to formulate a rearranged target for England.
It transpired that when play resumed four minutes before the final cut-off to complete the match, England needed a further 85 off 20 overs.
They got there easily, reaching 134 for four in 19.3 overs.
The weather interruption had loaded the odds in favour of the side batting second.
However Rixon wasn't happy at the decision to get the game started last Sunday.
For a one-day game to count, each team must bat a minimum 25 overs and for that to happen at Eden Park, play had to restart by 4.56pm in order to give England that many overs to bat.
"I know in Australia they would not have played under those circumstances, with four minutes to go and one side distinctly advantaged," former Australian test player Rixon said yesterday.
"They wouldn't have played and I'm sure other countries would have been the same."
Rixon's point is that with a welter of various permutations used around the world to decide how to complete a one-day game it is time one method was used everywhere.
"I think basically we need to be consistent," he said.
"It's up to the umpires. They run the game in the middle and we have to live by the laws.
"But I'd like to think somewhere along the way there'd be consistency in all countries, then we'd have no problem with the rules."
The method in use during this series is simply a breakdown of comparative run rates.
On England's tour of Zimbabwe, en route to New Zealand, they used a plan known as the Duckworth-Lewis system, named after two English university lecturers who devised the plan.
It is a more complicated method, but essentially takes into account the number of wickets that have fallen during the second innings up until the rain stoppage.
Under that system, England's target last Sunday would have been 164 off 26 overs, or 117 off the final 20 overs.
That would have meant a fairer contest, and increased the prospects of a win for the team bowling second.
